title: Norbert (6 June)
hook: a courtier knocked from his horse by lightning who founded the Premonstratensians

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kevin of Glendalough, and the bird in his open hand. Your line was the blackbird. Who did you stay still for? Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

Lightning, on a country road. Below it, a rider in fine clothes, on his way somewhere that matters to him. The storm breaks right overhead. A bolt strikes the ground in front of the horse, the horse rears, and the rider is thrown into the mud. He lies there, stunned, rain on his face, and, the story goes, he hears a voice. Yesterday's saint never moved. Today's saint gets moved, hard. Today, Norbert.
screen: `A RIDER IN FINE CLOTHES.` → `LIGHTNING ON THE ROAD.` → `THROWN INTO THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Norbert was a nobleman and a cleric at court, in the German lands, with a comfortable life and good connections. Tradition remembers him as worldly: holding church positions without much interest in what they were for. Then came the storm. In the story, as he lay on the ground he asked what Paul had asked: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" And the answer that came back was a line from a psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "Turn away from evil and do good." No vision of angels, no long speech. A line he would have known by heart, suddenly aimed at him. The scene has an echo. Paintings show Paul thrown from a horse on the road to Damascus. But read Acts, and there's no horse. The Douay-Rheims says only: "And falling on the ground, he heard a voice." The horse comes from the painters. Norbert's story has a real one, and the echo is hard to miss. What did Norbert do with it? He didn't change overnight into someone else. He did penance, was ordained a priest, and started preaching, barefoot, tradition says, from town to town. Then, at a remote place in France called Prémontré, he gathered men to live as canons: priests who pray the hours together like monks but go out to serve parishes. From that place comes the long name of his order, the Premonstratensians. They're also called, more simply, the Norbertines. Later he became an archbishop and worked to reform the clergy, the very kind of comfortable churchman he had once been. In Norbert's story, conversion is not one bright moment, but a fall, a question, and a long life of answering it.
screen: `A COMFORTABLE COURTIER.` · `THE QUESTION: WHAT WILT THOU HAVE ME DO?` · `PAUL'S HORSE IS NOT IN ACTS.` · `A FALL, THEN A LONG ANSWER.` · then, large: `TURN AWAY FROM EVIL AND DO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish someone a good turning. Not an argument to win, just a turning you'd hope for them. Close your eyes for a moment. Bring to mind one person caught in something that's hurting them, or a habit, or a hardness. Maybe it's you. Hold them without lecturing. If you pray, you can ask quietly, as Norbert did, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? and leave space for an answer. If you don't, simply wish them a good turning, in their own time. The bell holds the time.
Norbert. A courtier thrown to the ground in a storm, who turned, preached, and founded the Norbertines at Prémontré.
Your line: knocked from his horse. Today, when something knocks your plans over, before you get back up, ask what it might be asking of you. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Saint Norbert is remembered on 6 June; the Norbertine (Premonstratensian) canons and their parishes and schools keep it as their founder's feast, often with Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours sung together.

what a scholar hears: the horse in Paul's conversion is from art, not Acts; Norbert's canons live by a rule of common prayer but serve parishes.

notes: Conversion scene (lightning, thrown from horse, the question and the psalm answer) follows the traditional Vita Norberti; confirm the psalm line is the one tradition gives.
Acts 9:6 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' is in the Douay-Rheims (from the Vulgate) though absent from some Greek manuscripts; confirm exact Challoner wording.
Psalm 33:15 in Douay-Rheims numbering (34:14 Hebrew numbering).
'Barefoot, tradition says': confirm. 'Later he became an archbishop' (Magdeburg) and reforming clergy: confirm wording.
Canons regular description ('pray the hours together like monks but go out to serve parishes'): confirm as fair.
Practice framed as a turning wished for someone, not proselytizing; Keeper to confirm tone.
